item.title: The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
item.description: This article outlines the different factions involved in the current debate surrounding artificial intelligence development, safety, and regulation.
item.content:encoded:
The debate over the potential benefits and safety risks of accelerating artificial intelligence development reached a crescendo this month, as supporters and critics of the technology clashed over warnings that increasingly powerful AI could pose existential risks to humanity.
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher-turned-whistleblower, publicly resigned from major AI firm Anthropic after a previous stint at OpenAI, accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Coxon's claims supercharged an ongoing debate over the potential damage AI could wreak on society and prompted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other AI CEOs to call for a slowdown in AI development.
Over the past two months, companies including OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed multiple incidents in which their AI agents accessed the internet when they weren't supposed to and carried out unapproved activities. In OpenAI's case, swarms of agents worked together to hack the open-source software platform Hugging Face and OpenAI itself, without alerting humans.
The debate over the safety of AI and whether and how it should be regulated is not a simple clash between two opposing sides. There are multiple factions with a variety of goals and assessments about the technology's promise, dangers and how it should be governed. Here are the main arguments shaping that debate.
### Effective accelerationists and the tech right
Those who have an aggressively optimistic worldview of AI are often referred to as effective accelerationists (sometimes shortened to e/acc) – a term reflecting their belief that AI should be rapidly advanced.
People belonging to the faction are emphatically optimistic about AI and its future benefits to society. They believe that the technology can propel medical advancements, boost economic productivity, increase living standards, and automate dangerous or undesirable work. To achieve this, they argue that AI development should be accelerated, not restricted.
Effective accelerationists' ideology overlaps with that of the "tech right", in that both camps wholeheartedly believe in accelerating AI development and deployment and minimize critics' concerns over safety and security.
However, the tech right takes a more nationalistic stance, championing U.S. dominance in the global AI race. Like effective accelerationists, they believe that AI research and deployment should be unencumbered by regulation, arguing that could slow innovation or allow adversarial governments such as China to overtake the U.S. in the AI race.
The tech right's philosophy is represented by figures such as former White House AI and cryptocurrency advisor David Sacks, whose views remain influential with the Trump administration. Other significant players include venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman. The three founded the Leading the Future super PAC to support pro-AI political candidates, and campaign against those who advocate for regulation.
Andreessen also penned a 2023 widely-read blog post titled "Why AI Will Save the World," in which he claimed that fears of AI triggering mass unemployment are overstated. He argued that previous waves of automation ultimately created more jobs and economic activity than they eliminated, and the fears of existential risk are overblown.
Recently, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are used by most AI companies, has emerged as one of the industry's leading voices pushing back against calls for a slowdown and urging a light regulatory approach.
### Populist right
AI has exposed an ideological split within President Trump's political coalition. While Trump and his advisers overwhelmingly favor accelerating AI, parts of his MAGA base believe the powerful corporations he has aligned himself with could undermine the U.S. economy.
Figures including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson have been vocal about potential job losses, the tech industry's political power, child safety and threats to traditional social and religious values.
This month, Bannon formed an unlikely partnership with independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a socialist, to call for significant restrictions on AI development, government oversight and corporate accountability at the Pro-Human Assembly conference in Washington, D.C.
Still, the two have differing stances on what any of those measures should look like. Sanders called for an immediate pause on AI development until clear safety rules are established by scientists, a permanent ban on the development of artificial "superintelligence" (AI systems that are more intelligent than humans in all domains), and an international treaty with China in an effort to avoid an AI arms race. Bannon, meanwhile, argued for slowing the pace of AI development, the formation of a national regulatory organization and for cutting off China from U.S. AI technology.
"So why are we letting the Chinese Communist Party drive us? Oh, we have to do this or China wins," said Bannon in his speech at the event in Washington. "We should quarantine now every aspect of the ecosystem of artificial intelligence away from the Chinese Communist Party today. We should cut them off."
### Safetyists
Safetyists are primarily concerned with the potential risks of the rapid advancement of AI. Their worries center on the possibility of catastrophic or existential outcomes, such as the death of humanity at the hands of autonomous machines.
High-profile members of the safetyist community include Geoffrey Hinton, who is commonly referred to as the "Godfather of AI" because of his pioneering work in deep learning that helped launch the modern era of AI. In recent years, Hinton, who previously worked at Google, has issued a series of warnings about existential risks associated with AI, particularly if an AI model surpasses human intelligence and becomes autonomous.
Another vocal AI safetyist is Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI and co-author of AI 2027, a paper published last year that discusses how super-intelligent AI could lead to human extinction by the mid-2030s.
### Effective altruists
Effective altruists (often shortened to "EA") generally believe in maximizing humanity's long-term welfare. The movement originally focused on material ways to reduce global poverty. But more recently, many EA thinkers have focused their concerns on the possibility of existential risks from advanced AI and other potential societal-scale disasters such as nuclear war, climate change and pandemics. They particularly worry about the consequences for future generations. People from the EA camp prioritize AI safety, alignment – which is the science of making sure AI systems behave in a way that is reflective of human values and in line with safety rules – and reducing the probability of catastrophic outcomes.
The key difference between EAs and safetyists is that EAs generally provide funding for AI safety research and risk mitigation, whereas safetyists are researchers and advocates undertaking AI safety work and publicly calling for regulation.
Other AI factions often derisively describe effective altruists as so-called "AI Doomers." EA has also become a focus of criticism from the Trump administration since Coxon's resignation from Anthropic.
"Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" said one Defense Department post this month.
Well-known people in the EA movement include Eliezer Yudkowsky, co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), which focuses on mathematical approaches to making advanced AI systems safe. He is also the author of Harry Potter fan fiction that helped popularize ideas associated with EA. Holden Karnofsky, an American entrepreneur and philanthropist, founded Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), an organization that funds causes central to the EA mission, including AI and biosecurity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is considered to be aligned with effective altruism. Karnofsky also works at Anthropic and is married to Daniela Amodei, who is a co-founder of Anthropic and the sister of Dario Amodei, the CEO.
Another high-profile supporter of the EA movement is Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded major cryptocurrency exchange FTX. In 2023, he was convicted of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to the misuse of customer and investor funds and is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence.
### AI ethics
The AI ethics camp argues that society should focus on the harms AI is already causing, rather than on hypothetical existential risks. Some proponents contend that emphasizing existential threats from a hypothetical future superintelligence can serve as a distraction from the more immediate harms and accountability issues surrounding AI today.
AI ethicists' concerns include how AI systems can be biased due to the content of their training data, for example, the ways in which AI facial recognition or job application systems might perpetuate existing societal biases. They are also concerned with how AI could be used to exploit workers and to enable mass surveillance, as well as about the environmental costs of data centers, autonomous weapons, and the concentration of power among technology companies.
A notable voice of the AI ethics faction is Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist and former co-lead of Google's Ethical AI team. Gebru left the company in 2020 because of a dispute with the company over a research paper she wrote exposing problems with large language models (LLMs), including their tendency to generate harmful or misleading language.
### AI as a normal technology
People belonging to the "AI as a Normal Technology" group reject both the utopian and dystopian narratives about AI. Instead, this faction sees AI as a powerful but ultimately normal technology, comparable to the internet or electricity. They believe the focus should be on understanding and regulating specific applications and harms instead of treating AI as an unprecedented threat or as a path to inevitable superintelligence.
Notable people associated with this worldview include Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and co-director of the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute. Li is famous for creating ImageNet, a vastly large dataset of images which provided the training data for large neural networks, which led to several major developments in AI.
Katie McQue's reporting is supported by the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, which is a grantee of Coefficient Giving. Neither Tarbell nor Coefficient have any editorial input into her work.

item.title: Indigenous communities, Belledune work together to build 'green energy hub'
item.description: Indigenous communities and the Port of Belledune are collaborating on a 'green energy hub' in New Brunswick, focusing on clean energy projects and First Nations' ownership.
item.content:encoded:
There was a lot of positive energy at the Atlantic Indigenous-Led Energy Symposium this week in Saint John, with about 500 people engaged in animated discussions about promising partnerships between Indigenous communities and non-Indigenous partners.
Karen Narvie, a band councillor at Eel River Bar First Nation (Ugpi’ganjig), has seen the relathionship shift from one that has been combative in the past to one that’s more constructive.
She credits two things: meaningful and early conversations on projects, and First Nations ownership stakes in energy-related projects that have been made possible though by federal financing programs introduced in the last decade or so.
"We're not a tick on the box,” said Narvie, who was a panellist at the symposium organized by the North Shore Mi’kmaq Tribal Council.
“We want to move past basic consultation and the checklist to actively support models that provide Indigenous communities with long-term revenue streams, decision-making power, and equity stakes."
Eel River Bar and Pabineau First Nation (Oinpegitjoig) are involved with private sector partners and the Port of Belledune on several projects underway or in consideration.
In connection with that project, there will be a new wood pellet plant, a partnership between Pabineau, Eel River Bar, Arbec Forest Products and Airex Energy from Quebec.
There’s also the potential for a battery plant and a small nuclear reactor that could ultimately lead to a plant that builds and exports SMRs.
Consultation over energy projects getting better, Indigenous energy leaders say
Both potential projects involve Eel River, Pabineau and outside companies.
Pabineau Chief Terry Richardson is an enthusiastic proponent of a green energy hub that could create jobs and protect the environment for First Nations communities that focus on projects that support future generations.
First Nations in New Brunswick want in on clean energy
“The key is seeing [which companies] want to come,” Richardson said. “But these [projects] are going to open up some great paying jobs, great opportunities for our youth who want to stay in the region.
"We talk about the next seven generations for the environment, but there's also the next seven generations for the economic side.”
Narvie said the green energy shift better aligns with First Nations values.
“With the projects that are coming into the Port of Belledune, there's a lot of clean energy with the transition from coal to wood pellets and even the [SMR] project that we're looking at,” Narvie said.
Jennifer Cleversey-Moffitt, the chief administrative officer with the Belledune Port Authority, says the shift toward green energy projects and meaningful engagement and partnerships with the area First Nations communities happened during a period of big local changes.
Cleversey-Moffitt said Belledune went through a court battle 10 years ago with First Nations communities in Quebec over a plan to bring Alberta oil by rail to the port for export.
The project proponents won the court challenge but didn’t proceed with the project.
Cleversey-Moffitt said the end result felt “yucky.”
“We can't go through litigation every single time a project comes across our desks,” she said.
“It's about meaningful relationships [with First Nations]. It's not transactional. It's about developing personal bonds and understanding the community and understanding the historical context of where some of the concerns come from.”
The community was also going through an economic transition, she said.
In 2016, the province announced its plan to phase out coal at the Belledune station. In 2019, the local smelter closed.
The Port of Belledune went through a strategy review process and ultimately decided it wanted to remain industrial but with a green focus, which suited Indigenous partners too.
“This was really a bit of a renaissance for the port to understand that we can still be industrial, but we're going to do it in a much cleaner, greener way,” Cleversey-Moffitt said.
“And we're going to do it in partnership with those communities in the area, including the rights holders.”
Narvie said the pursuit of green industrial opportunities will ultimately improve social and economic well-being in her community.
“A lot of our own revenue goes to job creation, goes to our elders, goes to our youth, goes to some of our education at universities and colleges or whatnot,” she said. “So we continue to help our community grow and to be better.”

item.title: Facing a 2-year wait, this P.E.I. couple borrowed $25K to get a hip replacement in Montreal
item.description: A P.E.I. couple borrowed $25,000 for a private hip replacement in Montreal due to long wait times, highlighting issues in Canada's healthcare system.
item.content:encoded:
Neil and Janet Payne call it "Le Hip Trip."
A year ago, the Kinkora, P.E.I., couple were facing a wait of about a year for Neil to get a hip replacement.
His right hip had been worn down by osteoarthritis, and a hike on Cape Breton’s Seawall Trail made the pain much worse.
"I stopped working in November when the X-rays came back, and [the doctor] just said your hip is totally gone and you need a replacement," Neil told This is P.E.I. podcast host Mitch Cormier.
This summer, after waiting nine months, the couple called again and were told Neil would likely have to wait another 12 to 15 months.
"We knew he couldn't do that," Janet said.
"Neil's a really active guy, and to watch him lose probably 25 to 35 pounds as a result of the intense hike, but also because of all this medication that he was on, he just turned into an old man that just couldn't do anything anymore."
Instead of waiting, the couple borrowed $25,000 and drove to a private clinic in Montreal.
Their story is one of many that show how long wait times are pushing Canadians to pay out of pocket for care, despite a lifetime of contributing through taxes.
Colin Craig, president of the Regina-based think-tank SecondStreet.org, said the underlying problem is a system that hasn’t changed much in decades.
"We as taxpayers pay so much money into the government each year in the name of health insurance, and they’re not living up to their end of the bargain," Craig said.
After researching the options, the Paynes settled on Montreal. But they didn’t have the money on hand.
"After all those years and kids, we didn’t have $25,000 just sitting around in the bank waiting for a hip," Janet said.
They turned to a line of credit, knowing it would delay retirement and add financial strain.
"Maybe that means I'll just work until I die," Janet said.
"I would rather make that choice and have some quality of life for Neil and myself and our family than to just accept the fact that we had to wait 15 more months and that he might not have been able to make it."
The experience at the private clinic in Montreal, they said, was efficient and personal.
Within about 48 hours of deciding to go, Janet had the logistics set. The clinic co-ordinated X‑rays, blood work and other pre-op tests on P.E.I.
"The care in the clinic was unreal," Neil said. "You get your own nurse while you’re there and everything."
Janet paid another $1,500 so Neil could stay overnight after the surgery. He was well enough to travel home the next day.
"It was the first part of the next stage of his life," she said.
In a statement to CBC News, Health P.E.I. said it cannot comment on specific patients, but said wait times for hip replacements are improving in some areas.
The median wait was 282 days in the first quarter of 2026-27, compared with 276 days during the same period last year. The 90th percentile wait — patients facing the longest waits — improved from 519 days to 476.
"While wait times remain longer than the [Canadian Institute for Health Information] standards, recent operational changes are helping us increase surgical volumes and improve access for Islanders," the statement reads.
Eighty-nine hip replacements were completed during the first quarter of 2026-27, up from 81 a year earlier. It said 33.7 per cent of completed cases met the national 182-day benchmark, up from 28.4 per cent.
Craig said there is a misconception that only wealthy Canadians can afford to pay privately when faced with long wait times.
He said polling by SecondStreet.org found about nine per cent of people making less than $60,000 a year had gone to another province or country and paid for treatment because of long waits at home. The figure was about 11 per cent among those making more than $100,000.
"There's not a big gap between the lower income people and higher income people. It's people of all incomes now that are doing this," Craig said.
He said Canada could look to European health systems where governments guarantee treatment within set timelines and may pay when patients have to seek care elsewhere, including at private clinics.
"In these other countries, what they do is they fund services for patients," he said. "We fund health-care systems, so a lot of our money gets wasted on bureaucracy."
One possible change, Craig said, would be to have public funding follow the patient rather than being tied to a particular institution.
"Anyone should be allowed to do it, provided that they have qualified staff," he said.
"It shouldn't matter if it's a non-profit clinic or a for-profit or if it's a government provider. If the patient chooses to get their surgery there, the money should follow the patient.
"They're going to get treated like customers. The customer service is going to … improve. You're going to have a little bit of competition, and you're going to incentivize the system to want to help more patients and spend less money on bureaucracy."
The Paynes say they remain strong supporters of publicly funded health care.
"But is there a way to make it more efficient? Can we do more with what we have? Because what's going on right now is just not acceptable. People are really suffering and dying," Janet said.
Today, Neil is back hiking and keeping up with his children and grandchildren.
"I'm pretty happy about it," he said. "If I was still on the waiting list, my next summer could have been screwed too. I could have been limping around until next summer."

item.title: AI leaders say they want safety, but on whose terms?
item.description: AI leaders advocate for industry safety standards, but experts suggest their proposals prioritize company interests and self-regulation over independent oversight.
item.content:encoded:
As anxiety mounts over artificial intelligence safety, a number of leaders who helm frontier labs have made clear that they want — and need — better industry standards to contain the potentially dangerous technology.
Yet, like any industry leader hoping to achieve the most favorable conditions for their companies, AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis are hoping to play a significant role in determining the standards they seek, say experts.
"I think what has happened recently is that they've fully come to terms with the fact that they actually can't keep these things safe," Anthony Aguirre, CEO and president of the Future of Life Institute told Mashable. The nonprofit organization focuses on preventing extreme large-scale risks of transformative technologies.
Yet, Aguirre added, the fresh candor comes with a catch: "Certainly they want to be in control of the process."
What that could look like for leading AI companies is self-regulation, along with transparency and accountability on their terms, plus assurances about antitrust law.
AI companies want artificial general intelligence
Aguirre said that despite recognizing perilous emergent safety concerns, major AI companies still won't abandon their goal of achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI.
This form of AI would match or exceed human intelligence, and it could lead to the replacement of many human jobs with automated ones along with the rise of AI decision makers overtaking human leadership, Aguirre explained.
"They want to sort of have a machine-run future," Aguirre said. "This is not something most people want."
Calls for pacing the frontier, as Amodei recently described in a personal essay on AI safety risks, don't involve pausing the pursuit of AGI.
Aguirre believes that's a mistake. Instead, he said AI companies should "totally change direction" away from trying to create AGI, though he realizes they'll likely refuse to do so.
What the AI companies want in exchange for safety standards
Self-regulation
Pete Furlong, senior manager of policy and research at the Center for Humane Technology, told Mashable that the industry has been pushing for self-regulation for some time. "We've seen them talk about the need for regulation in certain aspects, but I don't think their actions always necessarily back that up," he told Mashable. Furlong added that the top companies want to protect their "industry leader status" and may seek ways to operate in a "closed door system" without much public input on risks and solutions. In a July Substack post on safety, Google's Hassabis suggested the U.S. create a standards body modeled on existing federally overseen public-private partnerships or self-regulatory organizations. Using the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority as an example, Hassabis said the standards body would lead on developing model assessment protocols and collaborating with federal agencies specifically on national security testing. In his essay, Amodei wrote that Anthropic has supported "sensible and targeted AI regulation," particularly on transparency and third-party auditing. Acknowledging the lengthy process of passing laws, Amodei also backed a voluntary effort on behalf of AI companies to set standards subsequently verified by "embedded" third-party evaluators. He unilaterally committed Anthropic to relying on those evaluators in its safety work. Still, experts cautioned against accepting this safety measure at face value. "While AI developers' support for independent evaluation is a real step forward, additional mechanisms will be required for effective accountability," Matt O'Shaughnessy, senior technologist at the Center for Democracy and Technology's AI Governance Lab, told Mashable. He added that it would be a "net-negative for accountability" if AI oversight amounted only to independent assessments.
Limited transparency and accountability
Furlong credited Anthropic for recently releasing a comprehensive safety report on AI-enabled risks like bioweapons and mass surveillance. He also said it was "laudable" that OpenAI had independent researchers investigate the Hugging Face incident during which an OpenAI agent hacked another company. Yet, OpenAI also placed "significant restraints" on that investigation, including time-frame limits, Furlong said. While these are reasonable steps toward transparency, Furlong believes it's fair to expect more.
"It can't be entirely up to these companies to dictate the terms of their transparency," he said.
While OpenAI and Anthropic have both backed transparency in writing, Aguirre said AI companies' actions don't always align with their public stance.
"I think there is a big gap between what they're saying and what their lobbying groups behind closed doors do," Aguirre said.
The major AI companies have also fought attempts to hold them accountable for worst-case scenarios, like when a user consults their chatbot about committing a mass shooting, gets life-threatening medical advice from it, or confides in it about feeling suicidal and receives advice on how to take their own life.
"There's a lot of potential concerns around companies trying to skirt any sort of meaningful accountability," Furlong said.
Reassurance on antitrust law
As the leading AI companies convene to discuss safety problems and solutions, they also express worry that doing so could expose them to anti-trust lawsuits.
Amodei said in his recent essay that the government should mediate or enable standard-setting discussions. He added that the government needs to issue a "narrow waiver" permitting specific safety conversations.
Aguirre said he agrees with the companies in this instance. Provided the waiver is carefully written to apply to safety discussions, and not coordinated activity that would freeze out smaller AI companies, Aguirre believes it's reasonable to want clarity about antitrust laws.
Indeed, a class-action lawsuit filed this week by Trial Lawyers for Justice alleges that a coordinated slowdown by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceXAI violated antitrust law.
The main takeaway
Aguirre believes that while many AI leaders are legitimately worried about safety, their proposals don't offer a radically different vision of what comes next.
"These companies are building something that they know that they cannot keep safe or under control, and they're doing so without any of the normal oversight or regulation that we apply to every other potentially unsafe industry," Aguirre said. "They're asking us to let them do the same thing, but just help them out a little bit to do it a little bit more safely."
*Additional reporting by Chase DiBenedetto.*

item.title: Toronto's top chefs are taking up farming, bringing new meaning to farm-to-table dining
item.description: Several Toronto chefs are establishing their own farms to grow produce for their restaurants, enhancing the farm-to-table dining experience.
item.content:encoded:
Toronto’s top chefs are taking up farming, bringing new meaning to farm-to-table dining
Meet the Toronto restaurateurs buying plots of land and growing their own produce across Ontario.
Chefs tend to have a long list of things to do: Prep, chop, sauté. Plan menus, cook for a crowd, clean up afterwards. But some of the city’s top chefs are adding even more to their workload: Planting, watering, pruning. Raising and picking the freshest produce, seeing it through from seed to plate.
When you dine on tender gai lan greens, Chinese chives and juicy Japanese melon at high-end dim sum restaurant Lai Wah Heen, it’s likely been grown on their own Norfolk County farm.
Prime Seafood Palace on Queen West receives a steady stream of pristine tomatoes, garlic scapes, purple broccoli, camomile and Chioggia beets from Blue Goose Farms, owner Matty Matheson’s small-scale farm in Fort Erie. Much of the bounty gets preserved to keep Ontario flavours flowing in the winter months.
Is getting into agriculture easy? Absolutely not. But for these passionate chefs, growing your own produce offers irreplaceable flavours, supply-chain solutions and an abundance of creative freedom.
Here, meet five Toronto chefs-turned-farmers giving farm-to-table dining new meaning.
Lai Wah Heen’s Dragon Farm, Norfolk County
Lai Wah Heen chef Gary Yue and his wife, Ming, picked up a popular hobby during the pandemic: gardening. First, they tried fig trees, then started growing food for their family.
As their skills grew, Yue realized this could also solve his restaurant’s sourcing problems. It was difficult to get fresh Chinese ingredients on Canadian soil. Why not grow them?
Now, their homegrown fig leaves are wrapped around baked chicken or made into teas — Ming grows almost 600 different fig varieties. The farm has rare breeds of chicken and a koi pond — the restaurant’s signature koi-shaped dumplings are served in their honour.
They grow choy sum, Chinese chives, Goji leaves and water spinach.
The team soon realized farm vegetables just taste better. “Ontario’s climate is actually well suited for a lot of Cantonese vegetables,” says Lai Wah Heen’s beverage director Peony Cen. Grocery store gai lan is thicker-stemmed and more bitter than theirs, which tastes like what Yue grew up eating in China. “And the garlic is amazing — it’s robust, and so aromatic you can smell it from three feet away.”
Not everything grows as planned: The Szechuan peppercorn ended up tasting like basil. “It didn’t work in entrees like we anticipated,” says Cen, laughing. “But it’s perfect for our cocktails.”
Fall feasting: Cen’s favourite fall dish is amaranth leaves. “They have a beautiful earthy flavour and natural sweetness. I like to cook them very simply with garlic. When the vegetables have just come from the farm, you really don’t need to do too much.”
Prime Seafood Palace’s Blue Goose Farms, Fort Erie
A technicolour rainbow of produce emerges from Matty Matheson-owned Blue Goose Farms, the site of Matheson’s soon-to-launch YouTube series, Matty’s Farm. Tomatoes the size of a grapefruit. Zucchinis with golden blossoms. Blushing pink beets.
Every week, chef-turned-farmer Keenan McVey and his wife, Ashley (a flower savant), pull up produce, then text Prime Seafood Palace chef Coulson Armstrong to let him know what’s coming so he can start conjuring up the week’s menu.
“We get everything in by Tuesday, test the dishes, photograph them, cost it, print recipes, and communicate allergens so we can swap the full menu by Friday,” says Armstrong.
This process has to be nimble and creative. The realities of farming mean the supply chain is dictated (and sometimes derailed) by rain storms, droughts, heat swings or other unpredictable spanners.
It’s worth it, for gems like ginormous, heart-shaped oxheart tomatoes. “They’ve never even seen a fridge,” says Armstrong. “We season them right before service and serve them like pan con tomate with B.C. Dungeness crab and confited garlic from the farm.”
The farm-restaurant relationship took a while to figure out, especially what gets eaten in-season, and what gets preserved, fermented or turned into condiments for colder months. “There was so much trial and error,” Coulson says, laughing. “We would ferment something and a few weeks later realize, oh that is not good. I guess it goes in staff meal.”
Fall feasting: When hosting big family dinners, “I like to add florals and greens to dishes to dress them up,” says Armstrong. “It automatically makes everything look more special and thoughtful.”
Bar Ape’s Berry Farm, Mount Forest
James Carnevale, owner of St. Clair West gelato hot spot Bar Ape, started farming out of necessity. The supply chain for two of his favourite berries — Tayberry and black raspberry — dried up.
“I was begging farmers for all they had,” he says. “I got to the point where I was cold-calling farms that may or may not sell them.”
These are special berries, with stories and flavours worth preserving. Black raspberries are indigenous to the North East. “Tay berries are the original blackberry, they have this unique watermelon Jolly Rancher meets raspberry flavour,” says Carnevale.
So he started planting his own, on his dedicated plot on Hawthorne Organic Seed Farm in Mount Forest.
He won’t see the first fruit till next year. Until then, he’s committed to sourcing other rare berries and deep-cut fruit varieties, driving around the province to pick up apricots, Ozark plums, gooseberry, haskap berry, cold-hardy kiwis and golden raspberries. Our gelato habit thanks him.
Fall feasting: White Niagara peaches are a Bar Ape gelato star. “It’s night and day difference between a farm-fresh peach and a grocery store one.”
Grant Van Gameren’s Home Farm, PEC
In the early days of Covid, chef Grant Van Gameren — owner of Bar Isabel, Bar Raval, Quetzal, and the soon-to-open Casa Rubia — did as many do and decamped to Prince Edward County.
For his family, it was a needed change of pace. “The county forces you to slow down and appreciate a different way of life,” he says.
For his career, country life offered a new challenge. “Being a chef, we love to explore new avenues that bring us closer to our trade,” he says. “Learning to grow vegetables was an obvious extension of that.”
He’s taken to it. Fresh cabbage is cooked into pork ragu at his Picton spot Rosetta, and the last of his summer tomatoes and peppers will end up preserved at Casa Rubia. Next up? Watermelon that’s just beginning to ripen.
It’s not always easy, especially when fall hits. “It’s all seeds and sunshine until August sets in, then you’re basically a full-time weeder ‘til October.”
Fall feasting: “Last year, we spatchcocked a very large turkey and roasted it in a wood burning oven,” says van Gameren. “It was absolutely amazing. If you have a wood oven, remember they aren’t just for pizza!”
White Lily Farms, Uxbridge
When White Lily Diner owners Ben Denham and Ashley Lloyd started their Uxbridge farm, they had a lot to learn. “We were just throwing things at a wall to see what sticks,” laughs Denham. “It’s dangerous for a chef to be looking through seed catalogues! There are so many heirloom vegetables and varieties that have fallen by the wayside over the years.”
Six years later, White Lily Farms supplies 20 restaurants with some 200 crops, including Habanadas (a heatless habanero), Jimmy Nardello (an Italian frying pepper), Barbie-pink Japanese okra, and celtuce (a crunchy, nutty, cucumber-ish lettuce).
Along the way, they realized they really, really like farming. So they sold White Lily Diner and opened Sundays, an itty-bitty, farm-to-table restaurant in Uxbridge. “We were doing 200 covers a day with a two-person kitchen,” says Denham. “It wasn’t sustainable. Now, our decisions revolve around produce.”
When deciding on fall dinner, Denham has a simple tip: “Ask the growers at the farmer’s market what they’re cooking! They’ll approach ingredients with so much care and intent.”
Fall feasting: Denham and Lloyd will be serving up roasts, braises and coq au vin blanc topped with farm-fresh arugula pesto, or duck liver with poached rhubarb.

item.title: Why some Republicans are pushing for a diesel export ban, despite industry pushback
item.description: Some Republicans are proposing a ban on diesel fuel exports to lower domestic prices, leading to a debate between agricultural and energy interests.
item.content:encoded:
Support for banning diesel fuel exports — an idea Gov. Jeff Landry jumped on — swelled as vulnerable Republicans weighed the plan against a backdrop of a rising blue tide, which handicappers almost universally predicted last week would lead to Democrats replacing Republican majorities in Congress.
Republicans had been mulling the idea for a few days before Landry wrote his opinion on X.
But it was the tweet by U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley that really fueled the debate on Capitol Hill. The longtime Republican fretted because his ruby-red state of Iowa suddenly was in play, with diesel costing an average of $6.52 per gallon, up from $3.69 a year ago, according to the AAA.
In addition to farm equipment, diesel is the main fuel for the trucks that take groceries to market.
Republican senators have fallen into two opposing camps over what to do — a situation that has pitted two of President Donald Trump’s staunchest allies against each other: the agriculture and energy sectors.
The main industry in Iowa is agriculture. Louisiana’s top two industries are farming and energy.
Though they represent roughly 25,000 farms, the state’s two senators, Bill Cassidy, R-Baton Rouge, and John Kennedy, R-Madisonville, also count stillmen, pumpers, and other operators in the state’s 19 petroleum refining facilities among their constituencies. Both oppose a ban.
Kennedy told reporters: "Everything I've read tells me it won't do any good."
Landry straddled the state’s two largest industries, demanding an export pause for the farmers and relaxed regulations for the refiners.
Trump has sent conflicting signals.
Cabinet secretaries Scott Bessent, of the Treasury Department, and Brooke Rollins, of Agriculture, suggested the administration would soon stop selling diesel to other countries for 90 days to build up supplies that would lower the cost.
But the Trump administration quickly backed off those hints, sending Energy Secretary Chris Wright to repeat variations on “We will not cease exports of U.S. diesel, but there may be some tweak” at multiple events last week.
If he wants to impose a ban, Trump can do so by calling a national emergency and using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act or the Defense Production Act.
With five weeks out from the November 3 congressional midterms, the cost of fuel has become a huge sticking point for Republicans wanting to maintain their control of all governmental levers.
“The costs of groceries, gas, and healthcare rank as top pain points for the rural voters, who were surveyed over two weeks starting in mid-August,” according to an Associated Press/KFF survey of 2,000 farmers.
Rural voters are the backbone of Trump's base. In Louisiana, for instance, the cities of Baton Rouge, New Orleans and Shreveport backed Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential elections, but 16 rural parishes gave Trump three-quarters of their votes.
That seems to have translated into election outcomes that don’t favor Republicans retaining majorities in the House and, perhaps, the Senate.
“The most likely outcome in the House is that Democrats pick up five to 15 seats, resulting in Democrats holding 220 to 230 seats in 2027,” (the majority is reached at 218 seats, which is the total number of Republicans in the House today), The Cook Political Report said in an analysis Friday. “In the Senate, the current range of possible outcomes we see is Democrats netting between one and five seats; they must net four to win back control of the chamber.”
Lost GOP seats are not a concern for Louisiana — though Republicans in Texas are definitely worried and the party is spending fortunes to shore up candidates in usually safe red bastions of Mississippi, South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida.
The nation’s 130 refineries make the U.S. the single largest global source, according to the American Petroleum Institute, producing about 1.6 billion of the 8 billion barrels traded daily on the world’s market. About 70% of the nation’s diesel stays at home to service the domestic market.
Professor Greg Upton, of LSU’s Energy Institute, explains that, very generally, a barrel of crude oil goes into the same piece of equipment that uses heat to separate the various petroleum products and produce kerosene, gasoline, jet fuel, diesel and other products including asphalt for roads.
Just how effective the export ban would be depends on how the refiners recalculate their equipment. Shifting product yields could put downward price pressure on gasoline.
“On the other hand, if refiners cannot find sufficient domestic demand or storage for diesel that would otherwise have been exported, they could respond by reducing overall refinery runs,” Upton said.
That scenario could raise prices.
Email Mark Ballard at mballard@theadvocate.com.

item.title: XbotGo Falcon review: A soccer dad's search for the perfect AI sports tracking camera
item.description: This article reviews the XbotGo Falcon, an AI sports tracking camera, highlighting its subscription-free model and 4K recording capabilities for parents and coaches.
item.content:encoded:
The Bottom Line
If you're looking for a sports tracking camera that requires some manual input but doesn't require a subscription, XbotGo Falcon is a must-try. The 4K AI camera is a smart pick for parents and coaches.
Your kids caught World Cup fever and now you'll be spending your weekends every fall and spring at the soccer field. Take it from a longtime soccer dad — you're going to love it.
In fact, you're going to get so wrapped up in this beautiful game that you're going to want to record those games for posterity. Here's another lesson this veteran soccer parent learned the hard way: You're not going to want to hold your arm up for an hour to record the match. Your arm will get tired, and you may find yourself paying more attention to your smartphone than to the moment itself.
That's where a sports tracking camera comes in. You set the camera up on a tripod on the sidelines of the pitch, hit record, and sit back and enjoy watching the game. The sports-tracking camera follows all the action, with an assist from AI.
For most parents, there's been one AI sports tracking camera that has risen above the rest: The XbotGo Falcon. And Mashable spent the last soccer season testing the camera out.
The problem with most sports tracking cameras
You may have heard of some of the big players in the space like Veo and Trace. Why not just go with those?
There's no doubt that Veo and Trace sports cameras have really good output. But, go take a look at their price pages. You'll find that you're spending hundreds of dollars on a camera that you can't even use without a subscription service, which often costs hundreds more per year. Before you know it, you're spending thousands of dollars annually. These services are more in line for soccer clubs, schools, leagues, or other situations where you're recording multiple teams and players on a regular basis.
You're just one parent. You have one (or at most a handful) of kids who play. You don't or can't spend that much on the camera, nor do you need anything fancy with player analytics and other bells and whistles. You just want to capture your kid making a great play or scoring a goal to share with the family.
XbotGo Falcon: No subscription required
I have long been searching for the perfect sports tracking camera. One where I can set it up and trust that it will reliably record the game, follow the action, and not require a subscription.
This is where the XbotGo Falcon sets itself apart from other AI sports tracking cameras
So, why doesn't the XbotGo Falcon require a subscription? Sports cameras like Veo and Trace basically record the entire length of the field, upload the footage to the company's servers, and then track the action within the footage after the game. XbotGo Falcon avoids those post-processing costs, as the device actually physically moves left and right, up and down, and zooms in and out during the game.
XbotGo is a fairly new company that strictly makes AI auto-tracking sports cameras and related products. The company found success in 2024 with the XbotGo Chameleon, a tracking device that required a user's smartphone to record. In March 2026, XbotGo released its next-generation AI tracking camera, the XbotGo Falcon.
XbotGo Falcon price
The XbotGo Falcon currently retails for $799.
There will no doubt be some initial sticker shock at the retail price. But, again, you need to look at its competitors.
The Veo camera, for example, costs $1,299 just for the device, followed by a minimum of $84 per month for their Starter base plan. Paying $799 once is certainly a lot less than $2,298 upfront, followed by $999 every year after that.
You will also need to factor in the price for a tripod of at least 13 feet or more. XbotGo sells one for $189.99, but you don't necessarily need theirs. However, it's a must-have accessory, which I'll get to in a little bit.
XbotGo Falcon: By the numbers
Here are the key specifications to know:
XbotGo Falcon vs. XbotGo Chameleon
Technically, both the XbotGo Chameleon and XbotGo Falcon have a camera built into the device. But that camera is for the tracking technology that follows the action on the field. The XbotGo Falcon has a second camera built in that actually records the game instead of using a smartphone to do that, as required by the XbotGo Chameleon.
XbotGo still sells the XbotGo Chameleon at around $300 for people who prefer that more affordable option. Also, some users prefer the XbotGo Chameleon, as you technically upgrade the camera quality as you upgrade your iPhone, by attaching the smartphone to the device to record.
However, having also spent multiple seasons using the XbotGo Chameleon, the XbotGo Falcon would be my go-to for a few reasons
First of all, having my smartphone available while using the XbotGo Falcon is huge. I can use my smartphone as a remote to monitor the XbotGo Falcon in case I need to pan or zoom the camera if it gets lost in the action. The XbotGo Chameleon requires that you attach your iPhone to the device. And while the Chameleon also offers remote usage with a second smartphone, how often do you have two smartphones on you? I know I don't.
In addition, the XbotGo Falcon footage is a crisp, clear 4K from a 1/1.8-inch Sony CMOS sensor. I can't imagine getting much more out of a smartphone camera anytime soon. The quality also means the files are fairly big. My 128GB iPhone is already nearly full from everything else. I would be unable to store much on it, and I'd have to spend time managing and moving files around after every other game. Having the ability to swap MicroSD cards is a huge draw to the XbotGo Falcon.
Using the XBotGo Falcon
The first thing you'll notice when getting the XbotGo Falcon is, well, its size. It's big, and it comes in a nice big carrying case as well. Its size is especially standout if you're upgrading from the much more compact XbotGo Chameleon.
To set up the device, you do need to sync the XbotGo Falcon hardware with the XbotGo app on your smartphone. The app is used to set up the recording, monitor the camera during the game, manually control the camera's movements, and update the device itself when XbotGo pushes out a firmware update. During your initial setup, there will most definitely be a firmware update so be sure to give yourself some time before you need to use the device.
From there, you pick your sport.
XbotGo says the Falcon is compatible with recording nine different sports, which include soccer, basketball, ice hockey, handball, tennis, pickleball, lacrosse, badminton, and volleyball. There are also three additional sports in beta — American football, rugby, and flag football.
For my XbotGo Falcon review, I focused on capturing soccer. Due to the larger field, this really pushes the tracking capabilities to the limit.
Once you've selected all the necessary settings, the camera will start to spin as it calibrates. Place the XbotGo Falcon on your tripod, which should be set up a few feet from the sideline near the midfield. Then, extend the tripod to at least around 12 feet in the air. The higher the better.
Users can add a scoreboard, set up a livestream of the event, record pan, tilt, and zoom manually during the game, and monitor what the camera is capturing, all from the XbotGo app.
And that's pretty much it. The XbotGo Falcon features physical buttons on the device for quick record options, but I prefer to use the smartphone to record, as the camera is already many feet in the air at kickoff.
Controlling the camera remotely is as simple as tapping on a sidebar menu option to call up an on-screen joystick, which allows the user to move the device around.
XbotGo Falcon performance
I tested the XbotGo Falcon to record at least a half dozen youth soccer games from full-field 11 versus 11 matches to smaller pitches for 9 versus 9 games.
So, how did it do? Most importantly, how was the tracking?
I was able to trust the AI tracking capabilities for the vast majority of each game. When referring to my iPhone to monitor the XbotGo Falcon, it properly tracked the game at least nine out of 10 times. In fact, I would say I only had to remotely control the device with my phone once or twice per game. Sometimes, I didn't have to touch the manual controls at all.
The camera produced very high-quality footage, too. In fact, recording in 4K allowed me to manually zoom even further using my editing software to get closer to the action when clipping highlights and still have clear HQ quality when exporting the punched-in clip.
Due to connectivity issues on my end at the fields, I was not able to test out the livestream capabilities in the proper setting. Personally, I prefer to record the games as the footage quality really matters when recording at a distance. Any sort of lower video quality due to livestream connectivity issues from your cellular or internet service provider will drastically reduce the watchability of the game. In addition, you'll most likely be clipping highlights from the full video rather than regularly watching the entire match, so again, the focus on the local recording is key for me.
XbotGo Falcon issues
Now, as great as my time with it was, there are some negatives with the XbotGo Falcon.
First, for those looking to buy a sports-tracking camera that's completely hands-off, the XbotGo Falcon will disappoint. Yes, it is mostly hands off in my experience, but it's also not "set it and forget it." While you don't need to monitor the recording like you would if you were holding a camera, there are clear points in a soccer match where you'll have to check if the XbotGo Falcon is keeping up.
For example, the XbotGo Falcon seems to struggle with goal kicks, corner kicks, and penalty kicks. There's something about the lack of typical back-and-forth movement on the pitch that causes the device to seemingly try to find it sometimes. I've unfortunately experienced missed penalties to the point where I would just use my iPhone to record the penalty and leave everything else to the XbotGo Falcon.
There is another limitation to the XbotGo Falcon, which really isn't the device's fault. At a youth soccer game, there are going to be kids off to the sidelines practicing while they wait for their game. There may also be more than one field at a location with multiple games going on. If any of this is in the view of the XbotGo Falcon, the camera will often get confused.
I will say XbotGo devices are now much better at dealing with distractions thanks to recent firmware updates, which added the ability to draw field boundaries so your Falcon doesn't stray. However, I had an issue where the Falcon was focused on one side of the field as a free kick was set up, a ball being used on the sideline rolled onto the field with a kid in tow on the opposite side of the field, and the Falcon spun around to catch that while missing the goal scored off the free kick.
With that said, the XbotGo Falcon does catch the action most of the time. In fact, remember when I mentioned the necessity of a big tripod? Most of the complaints I've seen online regarding its performance mainly revolve around the fact that many users just don't seem to raise the tripod high enough. The XbotGo Falcon needs to basically hover high over the pitch at almost a bird's eye view to get the best performance from it. It needs to see everything in order to track and capture it. If you put it too low, it will not track to the best of its abilities.
I also faced one weird issue with the XbotGo Falcon that appears to be a one-off, but I have to mention it.
During the very first game with the camera, it inexplicably stopped recording with 20 minutes left to go in a 60-minute game. There was no battery life issue or lack of SD card space. The device just stopped recording. At first, I thought it had something to do with moving out of range of the device with my synced iPhone monitor, but XbotGo told me that wasn't the case. Their logs oddly showed that a second smartphone synced with the device, and that device stopped the recording. It seems unlikely that another individual knew I was using an XbotGo device, downloaded the XbotGo app, and synced it with my device to stop it. While I never figured out exactly what happened, the device never stopped recording again.
Finally, aside from tracking issues, there is one persistent complaint among users: the watermark on the videos. There is a decent-sized XbotGo Falcon logo embedded on the lower right-hand side of all videos taken with the camera. There is no way to remove it. That's right. There's not even an option to pay extra. For me personally, I didn't find it intrusive. You can always put your own logo over the XbotGo Falcon watermark, and I never found it in the way of any of my videos. However, it is odd that it is there no matter what.
The bottom line: Is the XbotGo Falcon worth it?
This soccer dad was happy with his experience.
I can see why the XbotGo Falcon is hands down the most popular sports tracking camera on the market without a subscription. While it is pricey, it's nowhere near as costly as the ongoing fees its competitors charge.
However, there are tradeoffs, too. The fact that the XbotGo Falcon has to physically follow the action means that it will sometimes miss a moment. At the same time, the ability to monitor the camera from your smartphone is extremely useful and means you can manually guide it along, too.
One thing I will say: The company is very proactive when it comes to releasing firmware updates, which often add brand new features and fix ongoing performance issues. It's a huge plus in my opinion, which should make you feel secure in knowing that there's significant support behind the product.
Is it the perfect sports tracking camera I've been searching for? No. But it's getting there.
All in all, if you're tired of holding up a smartphone camera for an hour at a time, I suggest you give the XbotGo Falcon a try.
