item.title: I tested Belkin's 'semi-solid-state' battery — and it's the best iPhone portable charger I've ever used
item.description: This article reviews Belkin's new 'semi-solid-state' magnetic power bank, highlighting its slim design, lightweight, and Qi2 wireless charging capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
I'm a big fan of magnetic phone accessories, especially when it involves MagSafe-compatible wireless charging. Portable battery packs are great, but the reliance on cables is not something I will ever be happy about. Switching to wireless charging, and using magnets to keep everything in place, means that problem is eliminated — though it's not ideal that those batteries add a bunch of bulk and weight to your phone.
Belkin's newest magnetic battery pack, UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank with BoostSolid Cell, helps to eliminate that problem. The "Semi Solid State" battery design is significantly thinner and lighter than you might expect, which makes a surprising amount of difference for comfort. However, that also comes at the cost of overall capacity, which may or not be a dealbreaker.
Belkin's new Semi-Solid-State battery pack is thinner and lighter than any magnetic battery pack I've ever used. While the relatively low capacity might be a problem for some, it is an absolute joy to use for those reasons. It offers 15W Qi2 wireless charging on the go and built-in temperature management technology.
What the heck is a 'semi-solid-state' battery?
You may be wondering what Semi-Solid-State actually means. The idea of solid-state batteries is nothing new, since those offer power without any of the chemical movements and reactions.
According to Belkin, this "semi-solid" design utilizes a gel-like layer alongside a liquid electrolyte. The company hasn't gone into the specifics of how everything works, but the design enables a slimmer and more compact design, greater longevity and a much lower risk of overheating. That should help improve the overall safety of using these batteries, and considering the clampdown by airlines in recent months, that's definitely a good thing.
Speaking of airlines, Belkin says that the $70 UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank has been built to comply with standard safety requirements, and the TSA's carry-on guidance. Though this doesn't necessarily mean that you are cleared to use this one in the air. Each airline has their own policies, and you need to be aware of them before you travel.
The battery itself is Qi2 certified, offering up to 15W charging speeds on compatible phones. Wired USB-C charging is also available if you have a cable, with speeds up to 7.5W. The battery itself recharges at up to 22.5W. Naturally, being magnetic, it snaps onto the back of your phone — whether it has built-in magnets or you're using a special case.
Materials-wise, you've got a battery that is a mix of metal and rubber, which is not exactly uncommon in magnetic batteries, though the actual size of the thing is arguably where its biggest strength lies.
How does it compare to my existing magnetic power bank?
The magnetic battery pack I use most of the time is UGreen's 10,000 mAh magnetic power pack. It's a fairly cheap option, which means it isn't officially certified as MagSafe or Qi2 — it's just a regular wireless charger with a MagSafe-compatible connection. That means it's slow, and it has a habit of getting pretty hot.
UGreen's model is 0.79-inches thick, which is more than double Belkin's 0.35-inches. It's also heavier, weighing 7.9 ounces compared to 4.4 ounces for the Belkin. The UGreen battery is actually heavier and thicker than an iPhone 17 Pro (0.35-inches and 7.27 ounces), and only slightly lighter than the iPhone 17 Pro Max (8.33 ounces).
The UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank is still going to add thickness and weight to your phone. However, it is a lot more comfortable and convenient to use compared to the bulky UGreen option I've been using.
The downside is that it the Belkin has half the capacity of the UGreen. 10,000 mAh is enough to charge just about every phone at least once — and often more. 5,000 mAh doesn't go quite as far, but it's no small amount of power. It's enough to recharge a lot of phones in full, and enough to add a significant amount of power to others.
Personally, while I like to overprepare and make sure I have more than enough energy to keep me going, I'll admit that 10,000 mAh is a bit overkill for most situations. So long as you have enough power to make it through the day, and get back to a home charger, then what does it matter how much of a reserve you have?
In terms of charging and heat, I decided to test the two batteries on my iPhone 17 Pro Max starting at 47% charge. The Belkin battery restored 10%, bringing the total to 57% in that time, while the UGreen battery brought the charge to 54% — a 7% increase. It's not a huge amount of difference, but over the course of many hours that will add up.
As for heat, the Belkin battery definitely felt warmer, but a quick check with a thermal camera saw the temperature peak at just under 95 degrees Fahrenheit. The UGreen battery didn't feel nearly as warm, but the thermal imaging revealed that a small part of the battery had risen to just shy of 97 degrees. That's not a huge difference, but you do have to remember that the UGreen charger is going much more slowly — and I did feel that heat start to add up over extended charging sessions.
Wireless charging is always going to produce some heat if you don't have some sort of active cooling system. The Belkin UltraCharge does get warm, but it doesn't get too hot, which is quite nice.
Bottom line
I really like the Belkin UltraCharge Pro Magnetic Power Bank. Not specifically because it's a semi-solid-state battery, but because it manages to do all the things you need from a portable battery pack. It's slim and lightweight, with the magnetic connection making it incredibly easy to recharge your phone. Plus, the 15W Qi2 speeds mean it's fairly speedy as far as wireless charging goes.
Admittedly, the 5,000 mAh capacity would be enough to make me hesitate on buying one for myself — especially with a $70 price tag. You can buy wired battery packs that offer four times the capacity for similar prices, if not less. Still, you can't fault the Belkin for convenience or comfort, and that premium might be worth it if you regularly find that you need to top off your phone on the move.

item.title: City, township to work on replacing joint development agreement
item.description: Logan City Council and Falls Township trustees are discussing canceling and replacing a 25-year-old economic development agreement that has been largely ineffective.
item.content:encoded:
LOGAN, Ohio – Members of Logan City Council met on Monday morning with Falls Township trustees, to talk about the possible cancellation and replacement of an economic development agreement that was signed by the two governments almost 25 years ago, but seems to have mostly been gathering dust since then.
The Falls Township-City of Logan Cooperative Economic Development Agreement (CEDA) applies to multiple sections of the township, including all the township territory that overlaps the city. It covers such issues as new annexations into the city, the provision of city services, and the sharing of tax revenues.
Regarding the lodging or “bed” tax, for example, the CEDA says that once the agreement is in effect the township will continue to receive the amount of this tax that it already gets from rental units that are located in both the city and the township, but that going forward any bed tax revenues from new rental businesses created in the agreement area will be split half and half between city and township.
To judge from Monday’s meeting, however, the agreement has not accomplished much to speak of in the way of economic development since it was signed in 2002, and may have been largely ignored for much of that time.
James Martin, chair of council’s planning and annexation committee, noted that the agreement requires such things as ongoing cooperation, regular meetings, and joint planning between the two parties, but that “based on the records available to us, much of that has not been maintained and cannot be demonstrated.”
Given that the agreement seems to have been something of a dead letter, he suggested, it should be replaced with an agreement more attuned to the current realities of both city and township.
“We basically need to establish, what is the relationship we’ll have going forward,” Martin said.
Councilmember Jim Robinson, who was on council when the agreement was signed, added that there are some aspects about how it was originally presented, and the process of its adoption by council, that “just don’t make sense” to him.
He pointed out, for example, that rather than being signed by the president of council at the time, the agreement was signed for the city by Michael Walsh, listed on the document as “acting president” of the body. However, according to Robinson, the signer should have been council’s president pro tempore – a position that Robinson held at the time.
“If anyone signed that other than the president of council, it should have been the president pro tempore, which was me,” he said. “There is no such position as ‘acting president’ of council.”
In addition, he said, by his recollection the agreement as originally represented to council covered a significantly smaller area than the CEDA now on file.
“At the time it was presented to council, the only area that this was supposed to affect… was the area where the Olde Dutch Restaurant is – that strip, that hotel there… and going out and including the Grey Street area,” he said. But, he noted, the map now included in the CEDA “has the entire city. Any part of Falls Township that’s in the city, that overlaps… is all cross-hatched. It’s the whole city. And I’ll be honest with you – I don’t believe that I would have gone for that at that time.”
There is some urgency being felt by city officials about replacing the CEDA – or at least terminating it – because of one notable feature of the agreement: If it’s still in effect at the beginning of next year, it will automatically be renewed in its current form – for a term of a quarter-century.
“If we don’t do something with this, it’s going to be there for another 25 years,” city Service Director Bruce Walker told the township officials. “It’s not that we’re against having something like this. We would like to have an agreement to do away with it, and an agreement to work toward creating something that works for both of us.”
For their part, the trustees indicated they were amenable to working out a new development pact with the city.
The plan that came out of Monday’s meeting was for city Law Director Abby Saving to draw up a memorandum of understanding between the two entities, allowing for the existing CEDA to be canceled, thus taking some of the deadline pressure off for negotiating a new one. This will need to be presented to council and to the township board of trustees for their approvals.
Email at jphillips@logandaily.com

item.title: Some local leaders see opportunity in proposal for Nova Scotia's first data centre
item.description: A proposal for Nova Scotia's first data center by EverWind Fuels in Cape Breton is drawing mixed reactions from local leaders and environmental groups.
item.content:encoded:
Cape Breton could soon be home to Nova Scotia’s first data centre under a proposal by EverWind Fuels.
The plan is drawing mixed reactions, with local leaders welcoming potential economic gains while others raise concerns over water and energy use.
EverWind Fuels confirmed this week to CBC News that the green hydrogen company’s long-term plans include the construction of a data centre on EverWind’s property in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury, N.S.
The company has not provided a timeline for the application process or construction. Richmond County Warden Lois Landry confirmed that EverWind let the municipality know of its intentions “a couple of weeks ago” during a gathering of company officials and county representatives.
Landry is hopeful that a set of guidelines shared by Premier Tim Houston on social media two days ago, along with federal strategies involving data centre construction and municipal bylaws, will ensure that the proposal receives proper scrutiny.
At the same time, Landry says the industrial park that houses EverWind’s local operations is “open for business” and she is welcoming the potential economic opportunity for her municipality.
“We have 50-year-old infrastructure here in Richmond County,” the warden said.
“So we welcome economic opportunity, but to follow up on what the premier has been talking about, that’s not a blank cheque. But I think we should pursue all our options responsibly.”
Responding to Houston’s insistence that data centre proposals "protect water and the environment" through closed-loop cooling, Landry suggested Nova Scotia’s cooler climate will naturally ease the system's cooling demands.
“Anybody who thinks that you need the same amount of cooling in Point Tupper in January as you would in Texas — clearly, that’s a different kind of volume of heat that needs to be cooled,” Landry said.
Port Hawkesbury Mayor Brenda Chisholm-Beaton said she needs time to consult with town council before taking an official stance on the data centre proposal.
However, Landry expressed optimism that the reservoir currently shared by the town and county — Landrie Lake, located just outside Point Tupper — will not become part of any data centre’s needs without significant study from all three levels of government.
“We have an acute awareness of the water that we have available for any industry,” said Landry, pointing out that EverWind Fuels already taps into this reservoir for its green hydrogen production.
Jessica Cheung, the water and climate campaigner for The Council of Canadians, said the lack of information available from EverWind about its proposal should be worrying to Strait Area residents.
“EverWind hasn’t actually said how big it will be, or whether it’s going to be for AI or not, or how much water it’s going to use,” Cheung said Friday.
“And I think that the citizens that live there, and rely on the power and water that is there really, deserve to know that.”
She also questioned the fact that Landrie Lake’s residential customers in Point Tupper and Port Hawkesbury are already facing a yearly rate increase of 20 per cent for the next three years, while EverWind “has a flat rate of $74,000 for untreated water.”
From her office in Guelph, Ont., Cheung also encouraged Nova Scotia “to do this differently” in comparison to data centre developers in New Brunswick, Ontario, Alberta and across the United States.
“In June, Tim Houston had made it clear — and we were quite happy to see that — no more AI data funding would be made available until certain conditions came in place,” Cheung said.
“And then, suddenly, he’s taking a very different turn."

item.title: Angie Nixon Proposes Building Data Center on Mar-a-Lago
item.description: Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon proposes a moratorium on AI data centers and suggests building them on Mar-a-Lago, while also discussing her campaign's focus on economic issues and criticism of her own party.
item.content:encoded:
Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon believes the country should consider pausing the construction of new artificial intelligence data centers—and jokes that if companies insist on building them, they should start at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida.
Speaking to Newsweek in a wide-ranging interview, Nixon, a state representative who scored an upset victory in Florida's Democratic Senate primary last month, called for greater scrutiny of the rapidly expanding facilities amid concerns about their impact on electricity costs, water supplies and the environment.
"I think there needs to be a moratorium until more research is done," Nixon said. "Or if people want to build a data center, they should put it on Mar-a-Lago."
The issue is becoming increasingly politically salient as the AI boom drives a surge in proposed data centers across the country. Bipartisan opposition has emerged from communities concerned about their impact on electricity grids, water usage and utility bills.
Both Republican- and Democratic-led states have taken or proposed steps—including moratoriums—to address concerns, but Trump has downplayed the widespread unease. The president has repeatedly spoken out against AI regulations, referring to the backlash as a “hoax” and suggesting opposition will result in communities becoming “backwards and poor.”
Nixon told Newsweek she was not opposed to AI or technological innovation but wanted tougher guardrails around privacy, employment and the construction of data centers.
She also floated a proposal modeled loosely on Alaska's system of distributing revenue associated with its natural resources: requiring or creating a mechanism for communities affected by data centers to receive some form of financial benefit.
"Do we do what they do in Alaska, which is like, they give dividends to people who are impacted by the pipeline?" Nixon said. "Do we do the same thing for the now existing AI data centers?"
Nixon did not detail how such a program could work, but similar ideas are being considered already. Illinois lawmakers have proposed requiring certain data centers receiving state tax incentives to make payments to host communities, with some of the money benefiting homeowners through payments, credits or rebates, while proposals in New York would provide electricity-bill credits or energy improvements to residents near large data centers.
At the federal level, Democratic lawmakers have proposed taxing data centers to offset some of their economic and community impacts. While Nixon's Alaska comparison is not precise—the state's Permanent Fund invests mineral revenues and uses investment earnings to help fund annual dividends—the proposals share the principle of returning some economic benefit to communities affected by major development.
Beyond the raging debate over AI, Nixon's campaign is testing whether this year's political environment can make a state that has shifted sharply toward Republicans competitive again.
Trump, who has made Mar-a-Lago his primary residence, won Florida by about 13 percentage points in 2024, taking nearly 56 percent of the vote compared with Democrat Kamala Harris' roughly 43 percent. Republicans also now hold a commanding voter-registration advantage. As of August 31, Florida had about 5.65 million active registered Republicans compared with 4.10 million Democrats—a gap of more than 1.5 million voters.
The Cook Political Report currently rates the Florida Senate race Solid Republican, underscoring the scale of Nixon's challenge. The Sabato Crystal Ball shifted the race in the Democrat's favor this week from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican," Recent polling has produced a range of results—including two recent survey showing a dead heat.
A St. Pete Polls survey of 913 likely voters, conducted September 15-17, found Republican Senator Ashley Moody and Nixon effectively tied, 45.2 percent to 44.8 percent. A Change Research poll earlier in September also put the candidates at 47 percent each, although that survey was conducted for the Democratic-aligned Freedom Project USA.
Other surveys have shown Moody with a clearer advantage. Quantus Insights put her ahead 50.1 percent to 42.7 percent, while an InsiderAdvantage survey conducted September 20-21 found Moody at 49.3 percent and Nixon at 41.8 percent. Another poll released this week by Stetson University Center for Public Opinion Research showed the Republican ahead by 11 points, 51 percent to the Democrat's 40 percent.
There have also been signs this year that Florida voters are at least willing to cross traditional partisan lines in lower-turnout contests.
In March, Democrat Emily Gregory won a special election for Florida House District 87, which includes Mar-a-Lago, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Jon Maples by roughly 51 percent to 49 percent. Trump had carried the district in 2024. Democrat Brian Nathan separately flipped a Florida state Senate district that Trump had won by about 7 points.
Those results came amid a broader national environment that has recently favored Democrats. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in September found Democrats holding an 8-point advantage over Republicans among Americans asked which party they would support in the midterms, while Trump's approval rating stood at 32 percent. Democrats have also consistently overperformed in a slate of off-year and special elections across the country since Trump returned to office for his second term.
Republicans nevertheless enter November holding a 53 to 47 Senate majority, including the two independents who caucus with the Democratic side. Democrats, therefore, need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 if the rest of the map remains unchanged. Florida, however, is not currently considered among the central battlegrounds. A Nixon victory would signal a significant victory for Democrats, demonstrating that the Southern state increasingly viewed as a pro-Trump Republican stronghold is still in play.
Nixon's membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is another possible headwind the Senate candidate is seen by many to face. Florida is home to large communities of Cubans, Venezuelans and other Latin Americans, many of whom themselves fled, or grew up in families that fled socialism and communism. Moody has capitalized on these factors in her bid to get Florida voters behind her reelection campaign.
"The rise of Marxist organizations promoting communism should scare every American," the Republican incumbent wrote on X Friday. She urged Floridians to vote in the November midterm to prevent socialism from taking "root in our country."
Nixon joined the DSA in June but has repeatedly said she does not consider herself a socialist and does not agree with the organization's entire platform. She has specifically rejected calls to defund the police or abolish prisons, while supporting ending for-profit prisons.
Asked by Newsweek why she joined the organization despite rejecting the socialist label, Nixon pointed to its support for policies including universal healthcare, public education and affordable housing. She noted that she also joined the Working Families Party and became a lifetime NAACP member around the same period.
"For me, it was all hands on deck," Nixon said. "We have the ultra wealthy getting richer and richer and richer, and meanwhile, the rest of us are just breaking." Pressed on whether the DSA affiliation could hurt her with Florida's Cuban and Venezuelan communities, Nixon said she would not "insult the intelligence of the voters."
"They're smart and they do their research," she said, arguing Republicans were attempting to exploit voters' fears about socialism.
Moody has sought to make Nixon's DSA membership a defining contrast in the race. The issue has followed Nixon since her primary victory, and she said again this week that the campaign was "not about three letters," referring to DSA.
"There is no place in America that better understands the true cost of socialism and communism than Miami," Moody posted on social media earlier this month. "OUR FREE State of Florida will tell the Socialist Squad’s newest recruit, Angie Nixon, her destructive policies have no place in Florida," the Republican wrote.
Nixon also offered pointed criticism of her own party. Asked whether national and state Democrats were providing enough assistance after her primary victory, Nixon said they "could definitely give me more support."
"It's true what my husband has said sometimes," she added. "The Democratic Party and the Republican Party, they're just two different wings on the same bird."
Nixon said that some Democratic leaders receive money from the same interests that fund Republicans, adding that her own reliance on small-dollar donations made her a "threat" to that system. She also noted, however, the support she has received from prominent Democratic senators and progressive leaders, naming Senators Lisa Blunt Rochester, Kirsten Gillibrand, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren and Cory Booker.
Her criticism comes amid broader tensions within the Democratic Party ahead of November, particularly between progressive candidates and more establishment-aligned Democrats in several competitive races. While Democrats have overperformed in recent elections, there has been a strong strain of anti-establishment energy, with young and often more progressive candidates winning notable victories against incumbents.
This movement has also pointed its frustration at key Democratic leaders, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Some progressives have already begun calling for Schumer's ouster as leader. For her part, Nixon declined to commit to supporting Schumer but also did not rule it out.
"I'm going to run this race, I'm going to win, and then I'm going to assess who I want to vote for leader," she said. "And so it is going to be based on the vision that the folks have."
Nixon repeatedly returns her messaging to affordability concerns, saying that economic frustration could allow her to reach Floridians who previously supported Trump. Asked to identify three policies that would most directly lower household expenses, Nixon pointed to universal healthcare, repealing tariffs and universal childcare.
"People are going bankrupt because they're trying to stay alive," she said while advocating for universal healthcare.
On tariffs, Nixon described them as a tax on working families and argued that repealing them would reduce prices on everyday goods. She also contended that universal childcare would allow parents who left the workforce because of high childcare costs to return.
Nixon also called for eliminating federal taxes on Social Security benefits and recounted watching her 70-year-old mother return to work after retiring because her benefits did not stretch far enough.
"My mom's 70 years old and she should be enjoying her retirement," Nixon said. "She's worked her entire life."
Asked whether Trump had enacted any policy that she believed benefited working-class Americans, Nixon offered one concession: "Eggs are lower than what they were."
"That is the only thing that that man has done," she added, before criticizing the rest of his economic record.
Trump and Republicans have argued that their tax, trade and economic policies are designed to boost domestic production, increase investment and benefit American workers. Moody's campaign has sought to tie Nixon to the left wing of the Democratic Party, criticizing her agenda and warning that her economic vision would lead the country down a dangerous path.
Nixon also reiterated a position that puts her firmly on the progressive side of one of the Democratic Party's most divisive foreign policy debates. She told Newsweek she does not currently support sending U.S. money to Israel.
"At this moment, no, I do not support sending any money over to Israel," Nixon said.
She called for aggressive diplomacy and said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "needs to go," while arguing that Israelis and Palestinians must ultimately be brought together in pursuit of peace.
Pressed on concerns from Jewish and pro-Israel Democrats who view some anti-Israel rhetoric as antisemitic, Nixon drew a distinction between criticism of the Israeli government and hostility toward Jewish people.
"I push back on anti-Semitism," she said. "I believe Israelis have a right to exist."
"It's not anti-Semitic if I'm upset at their leadership," Nixon added. "I'm also upset at Donald Trump and his leadership in the administration. That does not make me anti-American."
Despite her sharp criticism of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Nixon said she would work with Democratic colleagues who accept support from the pro-Israel group if doing so helped advance policies she believes would benefit Floridians.
Throughout the interview, Nixon repeatedly targeted Moody, dubbing her "AI Ashley Moody" and accusing the Republican senator of siding with corporations and wealthy interests.
Nixon also argued that Trump had sold working-class voters a "pipe dream" and said some who backed him were now reconsidering their support amid frustration over costs.
But despite her repeated criticism of the president, Nixon rejected the idea that her campaign is primarily anti-Trump.
"I'm not pushing an anti-Trump message," she said. "I'm pushing a message about how people should decide what their economies and communities look like."
Her argument is that voters who may disagree with her ideologically could nevertheless be persuaded by an economic message centered on healthcare, housing, childcare and the cost of living. Whether that can overcome Florida's pronounced Republican shift remains an open question. The state's registration numbers, recent statewide election results and independent race ratings all favor Moody.
But Nixon is betting that the same voter dissatisfaction that has helped Democrats in special elections—including in the district surrounding Trump's own Florida home—can make a race few expected to be competitive considerably closer in November.

item.title: McDonald's revamp approved despite parking concerns at Hollywood Retail Park
item.description: Plans to modernize a McDonald's restaurant in Barrow, including a widened drive-thru and new ordering systems, have been approved despite parking concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Plans to modernise the McDonald's restaurant at Hollywood Retail Park in Barrow have been approved despite objections from neighbouring retailer Dunelm over the loss of parking spaces.
Westmorland and Furness Council granted planning permission on September 24, 2026, for a refurbishment of the fast food restaurant at Unit M, Hollywood Park, Hindpool Road.
The scheme will see the drive-thru lane widened to introduce side-by-side ordering, allowing two vehicles to place orders at the same time.
Other changes include the installation of a new "Fast Forward" booth for customers with delayed orders, relocated customer order displays, new canopies, alterations to kerb lines and a refresh of the building's external appearance.
Planning documents state the development is intended to improve traffic flow and operational efficiency rather than increase the restaurant's capacity.
A supporting statement submitted by McDonald's said the side-by-side ordering system would reduce waiting times, improve traffic circulation and shorten queues.
The company also said the Fast Forward booth could help reduce average drive-thru times by around 15 per cent by allowing customers with larger orders to pull forward while others continue through the lane.
The application attracted one objection from Dunelm, which occupies Unit B opposite the restaurant.
The soft furnishings retailer argued the development would result in the loss of parking spaces in one of the busiest areas of the retail park.
Dunelm's obbjection said: "The proposed development would mean the loss of at least 12 parking spaces - so a loss of amenity.
"The proposed development is in the busiest part of the retail park and so the loss of such a large number of car parking spaces in this area would be a material loss of amenity for our customers and those of our retail neighbours.
"We ask that the planning application be refused."
However, the council's planning officer concluded that the impact on parking would be limited.
The officer's report notes the proposal would result in the net loss of nine parking spaces, compared with a total of 657 spaces across the retail park.
Survey data submitted with the application showed there was substantial spare parking capacity even during busy periods.
The report also highlighted long-standing congestion issues associated with the restaurant's drive-thru, with queues sometimes extending back towards the nearby roundabout.
According to the assessment, the current layout accommodates around four to five vehicles before the ordering point, while the revised arrangement would increase that number to seven or eight vehicles within a similar distance.
Planning officers concluded that the additional stacking space should help reduce queues extending into the retail park.
Westmorland and Furness Council's highways team raised no objections to the development, stating it would not materially affect highway conditions.
In recommending approval, the planning officer said the proposal would improve traffic conditions, have an acceptable impact on parking provision and support investment in an existing business.
Permission was granted subject to standard conditions requiring the development to begin within three years and to be carried out in accordance with the approved plans.
